title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
lesson:
Write-ahead logging is the technique a database uses to make durable, crash-safe changes without paying the cost of a random disk write on every commit. Before a transaction's changes are applied to the actual data pages, the database first appends a small record describing each change to a sequential log on durable storage, and only reports the transaction as committed once those log records have been flushed to disk (an fsync). The data pages themselves can be updated later, lazily, in the background. The name comes from this ordering rule: the log write always happens ahead of the corresponding data-page write. Stated as two invariants, the log record for a change must reach stable storage before that change is allowed to overwrite a data page, and all of a transaction's log records must be on disk before the client is told the commit succeeded.

The payoff is crash recovery. If the process dies mid-flight, the data files can be left in an inconsistent state: some dirty pages flushed, others not, and some committed changes existing only in the log. On restart the database replays the log forward from the last known-good position, re-applying (redo) the changes of transactions that had committed and rolling back (undo) the changes of transactions that had not. Because the log is append-only, writing it is one cheap sequential I/O, whereas updating the scattered data pages in place would be many expensive random I/Os. So WAL delivers durability and higher write throughput at the same time, by turning a storm of random page writes into one sequential log write plus deferred, batched page flushes.

The log cannot grow forever, so the database periodically performs a checkpoint: it flushes all dirty pages up to some log position out to the data files, then records that position. Recovery can then start from the last checkpoint instead of the beginning of time, and log segments older than that checkpoint (and no longer needed for replication or archival) can be recycled or deleted. This is a tuning knob: frequent checkpoints keep recovery fast but add a steady background I/O load, while infrequent checkpoints reduce that load but lengthen how much log must be replayed after a crash.

The same log is the backbone of several other features. Streaming it to replicas is how leader-follower replication keeps followers in sync, replaying archived log up to a chosen timestamp gives point-in-time recovery, and change-data-capture tools tail the log to publish row-level changes to downstream systems. PostgreSQL calls it the WAL, MySQL's InnoDB engine has a redo log (plus separate undo log and binlog), and SQLite offers a WAL journaling mode. The pattern shows up well outside databases too: journaling filesystems and Raft's replicated log are the same idea of writing your intent durably before you act on it.

questions.prompt: What does "write-ahead" refer to in write-ahead logging?
options: The data pages are updated before the log, so the log is a backup copy
The log record describing a change is durably written before that change is applied to the data pages or acknowledged as committed
Writes are sent ahead to replicas before being applied locally
The database pre-allocates disk space ahead of every write
questions.explanation: The defining rule is ordering: the log record for a change reaches durable storage ahead of the data-page write and ahead of the commit acknowledgment.

questions.prompt: A transaction can safely be reported to the client as committed before its log records have been flushed to durable storage.
questions.explanation: The commit rule of WAL requires all of a transaction's log records to be on stable storage before the commit is acknowledged, otherwise a crash could lose an acknowledged transaction.

questions.prompt: To bound recovery time and let old log segments be reclaimed, a database periodically flushes dirty pages to the data files and records the log position it reached, an operation called a ____.
questions.explanation: A checkpoint lets recovery start from a recent log position instead of the beginning, and frees log written before it for recycling.

questions.prompt: Why does WAL typically improve write throughput compared to updating data pages in place on every commit?
options: It compresses the data pages before writing them
It skips writing the changes to disk entirely until shutdown
Appending to a sequential log is one cheap I/O, while data-page writes can then be batched and deferred instead of being many random I/Os
It moves all writes onto a separate faster network
questions.explanation: WAL converts many scattered random page writes into a single sequential log write plus deferred, batched page flushes.

questions.prompt: Order these steps of crash recovery using a write-ahead log, earliest first.
items: Committed changes recorded in the log are re-applied (redo) to the data files
The database process crashes with some committed changes present only in the log
Changes made by transactions that never committed are rolled back (undo)
On restart, the database scans the log forward from the last checkpoint
questions.explanation: Recovery starts after the crash, scans the log from the last checkpoint, redoes changes of committed transactions, then undoes changes of transactions that never committed.

questions.prompt: The same write-ahead log a database uses for crash recovery is also commonly streamed to followers to keep them in sync in leader-follower replication.
questions.explanation: Shipping the WAL to replicas, which replay it, is a standard way leader-follower replication keeps followers consistent with the leader.
